before: Unique identities make record lookup unambiguous. A repeated ID is a data problem even if the titles differ.
This exercise is a small pure JavaScript model. Its inputs are supplied directly; it does not receive live HTTP requests, operate a database, or deploy a service.
map extracts IDs. Set stores each distinct value once. If its size is smaller than the original list, at least one identity occurred more than once. IDs here are integers.

Read the function call hasDuplicateIds([{"id":1},{"id":2}]) from the inside out: the arguments supply the inputs, hasDuplicateIds runs the body once, and return sends its result back to the caller. console.log displays that result; it does not change it.
Two records have ID 3 and different titles. Are their IDs unique? Uniqueness concerns the ID field, independent of title or position.
after: Unique means each value appears only once. Notes need unique IDs so an ID identifies one record. Different titles do not make a repeated ID unique.
map creates an array containing each note's id. This exercise uses integer IDs. The notes and their fields stay unchanged.
A Set keeps each distinct value once. new Set(ids).size counts how many different IDs exist.
If the distinct count differs from the full count, at least one ID appeared more than once. Return true in that case. Empty input has no repeated IDs, so it returns false.
Complete hasDuplicateIds(notes). Compare the number of IDs with the number of distinct IDs. Do not delete duplicates or change the notes; just report whether any ID repeats.
